questions.text:
Geetha has a conjecture about integers, which is of the form
[latex]\forall x\left [P(x)\Rightarrow \exists yQ(x,y) \right ] [/latex]
where [latex]P[/latex] is a statement about integers, and [latex]Q[/latex] is a statement about pairs of integers. Which of the following (one or more) option(s) would imply Geetha's conjecture?
questions.solution:
Conjecture: for every x with P(x), some y makes Q(x, y) true.

- Option 1 talks about only one x [latex]\text{---}[/latex] does not imply it.
- Option 2: Q holds for all x and y, so for any x any y works [latex]\text{---}[/latex] implies it.
- Option 3: one fixed y works for every x with P(x), so such a y exists for each x [latex]\text{---}[/latex] implies it.
- Option 4 again talks about only one x [latex]\text{---}[/latex] does not imply it.

Answer: Options 2 and 3

questions.text:
The Lucas sequence [latex] L_n [/latex] is defined by the recurrence relation:
[latex] L_n=L_{n-1}+L_{n-2}, \; for \; n\geq 3, [/latex]
with [latex] L_1=1 \; and \; L_2=3 [/latex]
Which one of the options given is TRUE?
questions.solution:
Let [latex]\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}[/latex] and [latex]\psi=\frac{1-\sqrt5}{2}[/latex]. They satisfy [latex]x^2=x+1[/latex], [latex]\varphi+\psi=1[/latex], [latex]\varphi\psi=-1[/latex].

Check [latex]L_n=\varphi^n+\psi^n[/latex]:
- [latex]L_1=\varphi+\psi=1[/latex] True
- [latex]L_2=(\varphi+\psi)^2-2\varphi\psi=1+2=3[/latex] True
- It satisfies [latex]L_n=L_{n-1}+L_{n-2}[/latex] because both [latex]\varphi,\psi[/latex] satisfy [latex]x^2=x+1[/latex].

Answer: [latex]L_n=\left(\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\right)^n+\left(\frac{1-\sqrt5}{2}\right)^n[/latex]

questions.text: Which of the properties hold for the adjacency matrix [latex]A[/latex] of a simple undirected unweighted graph having [latex]n[/latex] vertices?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex](A^2)_{ii}=\sum_k a_{ik}a_{ki}[/latex] = number of neighbours of i = degree [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Path 1-2-3 (n = 3): [latex]A^2+I[/latex] has entry (1, 2) = 0, since there is no walk of length exactly 2 from 1 to 2 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Sum of entries [latex]\le2(n-1)[/latex] means at most [latex]n-1[/latex] edges. A triangle plus an isolated vertex (n = 4, 3 edges) still has a cycle [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Two disjoint edges on 4 vertices: every row has a 1, but the graph is disconnected [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: The diagonal entries of [latex]A^2[/latex] are the degrees of the vertices

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: The diagonal entries of [latex]A^2[/latex] are the degrees of the vertices of the graph.
If the graph is connected, then none of the entries of [latex]A^{n-1}+I_n[/latex]can be zero.
If the sum of all the elements of [latex]A[/latex] is at most 2(n-1), then the graph must be acyclic.
If there is at least a 1 in each of A's rows and columns, then the graph must be connected.

questions.text:
Consider the following recurrence:
[latex] \begin{aligned} f(1)&=1; \\ f(2n)&=2f(n)-1, & \text{for }n \geq 1; \\ f(2n+1)&=2f(n)+1, & \text{for }n \geq 1. \end{aligned}[/latex]
Then, which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Compute some values: f(1)=1, f(2)=1, f(3)=3, f(4)=1, f(5)=3, f(6)=5, f(7)=7, f(8)=1, f(10)=5, f(20)=9.

- [latex]f(2^n-1)=2^n-1[/latex]: f(1)=1, f(3)=3, f(7)=7 True (by induction [latex]f(2m+1)=2f(m)+1[/latex])
- [latex]f(2^n)=1[/latex]: [latex]f(2^n)=2f(2^{n-1})-1=2-1=1[/latex] True
- [latex]f(5\cdot2^n)=2^{n+1}+1[/latex]: f(5)=3, f(10)=5, f(20)=9 True
- [latex]f(2^n+1)=2^n+1[/latex]: f(5)=3 [latex]\ne[/latex] 5 False

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

questions.text:
The following simple undirected graph is referred to as the Peterson graph.

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Petersen graph: 10 vertices, 3-regular, no triangles or 4-cycles.

- Odd cycles (5-cycles) need 3 colours, and 3 are enough [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] chromatic number 3 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- It has no Hamiltonian cycle, but it does have a Hamiltonian path (outer cycle 4 vertices, then into the star) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- The given graph is also 3-regular on 10 vertices with girth 5, and is a known drawing of the Petersen graph [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- The largest independent set has size 4, not 3 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

options: The chromatic number of the graph is 3.
The graph has a Hamiltonian path.
The following graph is isomorphic to the Peterson graph.
The size of the largest independent set of the given graph is 3. (A subset of vertices of a graph form an independent set if no two vertices of the subset are adjacent.)
